Problem Set 2

EC 422: Economic Forecasting | Fall 2026

Author

Aidan Dugan

Published

October 16, 2026

GitHub repo: https://github.com/adugan10/ec422_ps2_dugan

Data

The data are seasonally adjusted monthly unemployment rates for the United States, Oregon, California, Texas, and New York. They come from the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) database and are identified by the series codes UNRATE, ORUR, CAUR, TXUR, and NYUR. The series were requested starting in January 1976. Because tq_get() may fail when accessing FRED, I use the unemp_raw.rds dataset provided by Professor Piger and stored in the project’s data folder, following his October 16 instructions.

# Use the data file Professor Piger provided as an email attachment.
# It must be saved inside this project as data/unemp_raw.rds.
unemp_raw <- read_rds("data/unemp_raw.rds")
head(unemp_raw)
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  symbol date       price
  <chr>  <date>     <dbl>
1 UNRATE 1976-01-01   7.9
2 UNRATE 1976-02-01   7.7
3 UNRATE 1976-03-01   7.6
4 UNRATE 1976-04-01   7.7
5 UNRATE 1976-05-01   7.4
6 UNRATE 1976-06-01   7.6

The saved observations cover January 1976 through August 2026. Each row represents a region in one month. The price field in the original data contains the unemployment rate.

Wrangling

First, I renamed the rate variable and mapped each FRED series code to a readable region name. I then filled October 2025 with September 2025’s value within each region, as instructed, before computing monthly changes in percentage points. I also created a restricted sample from January 2015 onward and separate summaries that exclude observations from 2020.

unemp <- unemp_raw |>
  rename(unemployment_rate = price) |>
  mutate(
    region = case_when(
      symbol == "UNRATE" ~ "United States",
      symbol == "ORUR"   ~ "Oregon",
      symbol == "CAUR"   ~ "California",
      symbol == "TXUR"   ~ "Texas",
      symbol == "NYUR"   ~ "New York"
    )
  )

# Represent any skipped month explicitly before filling October 2025.
unemp <- unemp |>
  group_by(region, symbol) |>
  complete(date = seq.Date(min(date), max(date), by = "month")) |>
  ungroup()

unemp <- unemp |>
  arrange(region, date) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  mutate(
    unemployment_rate = replace(
      unemployment_rate,
      date == as.Date("2025-10-01"),
      unemployment_rate[date == as.Date("2025-09-01")]
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

unemp <- unemp |>
  arrange(region, date) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  mutate(
    unemployment_rate_change = unemployment_rate - lag(unemployment_rate)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

unemp_recent <- unemp |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2015-01-01"))

unemp_summary <- unemp |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarize(
    mean_rate = mean(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_rate = min(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_rate = max(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

unemp_recent_summary <- unemp_recent |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarize(
    mean_rate = mean(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_rate = min(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_rate = max(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

unemp_top_increases <- unemp |>
  filter(!is.na(unemployment_rate_change)) |>
  slice_max(unemployment_rate_change, n = 5, with_ties = TRUE)

unemp_top_decreases <- unemp |>
  filter(!is.na(unemployment_rate_change)) |>
  slice_min(unemployment_rate_change, n = 5, with_ties = TRUE)

unemp_no_covid <- unemp |>
  filter(format(date, "%Y") != "2020")

unemp_top_increases_no_covid <- unemp_no_covid |>
  filter(!is.na(unemployment_rate_change)) |>
  slice_max(unemployment_rate_change, n = 5, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  select(region, date, unemployment_rate_change, unemployment_rate)

unemp_top_decreases_no_covid <- unemp_no_covid |>
  filter(!is.na(unemployment_rate_change)) |>
  slice_min(unemployment_rate_change, n = 5, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  select(region, date, unemployment_rate_change, unemployment_rate)

Visualization

Figure 1. Unemployment rates over time

The first chart puts the United States and four states on the same axes so their unemployment-rate levels and common turning points can be compared.

Figure 2. Unemployment rates in individual panels

Faceting the same monthly series makes it easier to trace each region’s pattern without overlapping lines.

Figure 3. Mean unemployment rates by region

The bars are ordered from the lowest to the highest full-sample average.

Figure 4. Size of monthly changes by region

For my additional plot, I compare the absolute month-to-month change in the unemployment rate across regions using boxplots. I chose this because the line plots show rate levels, while a distribution of monthly changes makes it easier to compare how much the unemployment rate typically moves from month to month.

Reflection

This assignment helped me get more comfortable using R to work with data. Using the provided data file made it easier to focus on organizing the data and creating the tables and graphs. One thing I had to pay more attention to was making sure the dates were in the right order when calculating monthly changes. I also thought it was interesting to see how excluding 2020 affected the results. Overall, I have a better understanding of how RStudio, Quarto, and GitHub work together.
